name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
description: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) is a large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research. The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consists of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages (German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish). The dataset also includes Language Models (LM) and baseline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models for all languages.
license: Public domain (derived from LibriVox and Project Gutenberg data released in the public domain)
creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert (Facebook AI Research)
inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
citeAs: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert. 'MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research.' arXiv preprint, December 22, 2020.
rai:dataCollection: Audiobooks were downloaded from LibriVox using data preparation tools available at the LibriLight open source library. Text sources for the audiobooks were downloaded from multiple domains including gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, and hathitrust.org for English, and various other sources for other languages. Some text extraction involved manual approaches including copying text from browsers, extracting from PDF/EPUB files using pdftotext, or writing HTML parsers. All audio data was downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For some languages, text sources for audiobooks were missing due to invalid links or pages redirecting to incorrect pages. For example, all text sources from the spiegel.de domain (accounting for 1/3rd of German audio data) were being redirected to an invalid page. Manual searches were conducted to find alternate sources for unavailable books.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Read audiobooks from LibriVox (audio) and corresponding book texts primarily from Project Gutenberg and other online sources (gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, hathitrust.org, projekt-gutenberg.de, zeno.org, spiegel.de, etc.).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Audio files were segmented into 10-20 second segments using trained acoustic models to generate Viterbi token sequences with timestamps, then splitting at the longest silence duration within the 10-20 sec range. Pseudo labels were generated using beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model. Transcript retrieval was performed by matching pseudo labels to source text using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams and Smith-Waterman alignment. Numbers in text were replaced with aligned words from pseudo labels. Heuristics were applied for handling hyphens and apostrophes. Candidate transcripts with WER > 40% between candidate transcript and pseudo label were filtered out.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text normalization included NFKC normalization, removal of unwanted characters (punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols), removal of end-of-line hyphens, and filtering of characters outside valid unicode ranges for each language's orthography. Books with corrupted metadata (missing title or speaker/author information) were removed. Multi-speaker audio chapters (e.g., 'Dramatic Reading') were removed. Only the latest version of books sharing the same authors and title but different versions was kept. Speakers were labeled by gender using an SVM gender classifier. Speakers with duration shorter than a threshold were assigned to training set. For language model data, books with title edit distance less than 2 from dev/test set books were removed, and books with more than 1% of 5-grams appearing in dev/test sets were also removed.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Transcripts were generated automatically via a pipeline: (1) pseudo labels generated by beam-search decoding with acoustic models, (2) transcript retrieval by matching pseudo labels to source book text using TF-IDF and Smith-Waterman alignment, (3) post-processing of numbers, hyphens, and apostrophes. For development and test sets, human transcribers listened to audio while reviewing the generated transcript and corrected 'clear and obvious' errors only, to avoid introducing bias.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: WER between generated transcript (GT) and human rated transcript (HRT) was measured for dev and test sets across all 8 languages. Error rates ranged from 1.93% (Spanish dev) to 12.64% (Portuguese dev), indicating varying levels of automatic transcript quality across languages.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: wav2letter@anywhere framework for streaming inference; Time-Depth Separable (TDS) Convolutions with Auto-Segmentation Criterion (ASG) loss for acoustic models; beam-search decoding with 4-gram language model for pseudo label generation; TF-IDF similarity on bigrams for document retrieval; Smith-Waterman alignment for transcript matching; SVM with RBF kernel gender classifier; KenLM toolkit for language model training; pdftotext for PDF/EPUB text extraction; num2words library considered but not used as primary solution
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is made freely available at http://www.openslr.org. Pretrained models and recipes are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/wav2letter. No explicit versioning or deprecation policy is described.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker gender information is included in the dataset. Speaker identities are present (speaker IDs). Audio data used for training acoustic models was completely de-identified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to open new avenues in ASR and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research by providing a large, freely available multilingual speech corpus. It promotes open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and in multilingual ASR, potentially benefiting speakers of multiple languages.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is derived from read audiobooks, which may not represent natural conversational speech. The gender classifier used to label speakers has varying accuracy across languages (95% on LibriSpeech, 96% on Dutch, 94% on Polish). There is significant imbalance in the amount of data across languages, with English having far more hours than other languages. The Dutch training set has a notable gender imbalance (9 male vs. 31 female speakers).
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset consists of read speech from audiobooks and may not generalize well to conversational or spontaneous speech. Polish has a high OOV rate of 13.39% in the language model, negatively impacting LM-decoded WER. The amount of data varies significantly across languages. Some audiobook text sources could not be retrieved, reducing coverage. The dataset is limited to 8 languages.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems; Text-to-Speech (TTS) research; multilingual speech research; low-resource ASR benchmarking (limited supervision sets of 10 hours, 1 hour, and six 10-minute sets provided per language); language model training and evaluation.
